what_its_for: Tacrolimus is a medicine that weakens your immune system to help prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted organ, such as a kidney, liver, or heart. It works by stopping your immune system from attacking the new organ.
how_to_take: Take tacrolimus exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the capsules or tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. Take your doses at the same times every day to keep the medicine working steadily in your body. You may take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way (with food or without food) every time. If you use the liquid form, measure your dose carefully with the measuring device provided — do not use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: Your dose is carefully calculated just for you based on your body weight, the type of transplant you had, and regular blood tests. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor will check your tacrolimus blood levels often and adjust your dose as needed. The extended-release versions (Astagraf XL and Envarsus XR) are taken only ONCE a day in the morning. The regular capsules (Prograf) are taken TWICE a day, about 12 hours apart.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is within a few hours of your usual time. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist right away.
storage: Store tacrolimus capsules and tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the medicine away from moisture and heat. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any medicine you no longer need.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice while taking tacrolimus — it can raise the level of the medicine in your blood to a dangerous level. Limit your time in the sun, wear protective clothing, and use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, because tacrolimus increases your risk of skin cancer. Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, since your immune system is weakened. Do not get any live vaccines (such as live flu vaccine, MMR, or chickenpox vaccine) without asking your doctor first. Talk to your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements, including St. John's Wort, as many drugs can interact with tacrolimus.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: signs of infection such as fever, chills, sore throat, or unusual tiredness; signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination, swelling in your legs or feet, or unusual weight gain; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst or frequent urination; numbness, tingling, or tremors (shaking) in your hands; severe headache, confusion, vision changes, or seizures; chest pain or trouble breathing; any unusual lumps or skin changes that could be a sign of cancer. Also call your doctor if you experience diarrhea or vomiting lasting more than one day, since this can affect how much medicine your body absorbs.
when_it_works: Tacrolimus starts working right away to protect your new organ. However, finding the right dose for your body can take several weeks. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to make sure your levels are in the right range — not too high (which can cause side effects) and not too low (which can lead to rejection). It is very important to keep taking this medicine every day, even if you feel well. Never stop taking tacrolimus without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects and may need closer monitoring. Tacrolimus is used in children after transplant but doses are carefully adjusted by weight and blood levels. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor immediately — tacrolimus can harm an unborn baby, but stopping the medicine can also put your transplanted organ at risk. Do not breastfeed while taking tacrolimus, as the medicine can pass into breast milk. People with liver problems may process this medicine more slowly and may need dose adjustments. If you have diabetes, tacrolimus can raise your blood sugar levels, so monitor your blood sugar closely and report any changes to your doctor.
